stories.headline: Coalition of 25 Democratic-Led States Sues Trump Administration Over New Global Tariffs
stories.summary:
A coalition of 25 Democratic-controlled states filed a lawsuit Monday in the U.S. Court of International Trade in New York challenging the Trump administration's latest round of global tariffs, which impose surcharges of 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners. The states argue the new tariffs are an unlawful attempt to resurrect a tariff regime the Supreme Court struck down earlier this year, using a different legal authority as pretext. They are asking the court to halt the tariffs and declare them illegal.

The Trump administration has defended the new tariffs, asserting they target countries that have not done enough to crack down on imports produced by forced labor. The White House and its supporters argue the president has broad authority to impose tariffs to protect national economic interests. The lawsuit adds to parallel legal challenges already filed by small businesses in recent days.

The case represents one of the most sweeping legal confrontations between Democratic-led states and the Trump administration over trade policy. If successful, the challenge could block tariffs affecting hundreds of billions of dollars in goods imported from dozens of trading partners, with significant implications for businesses and consumers nationwide.

stories.headline: Killer of Minnesota House Speaker Makes First State Court Appearance
stories.summary:
Vance Boelter, who is serving two life sentences plus 40 years in federal prison after pleading guilty to killing former Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband Mark, made his initial appearance Monday in Hennepin County state court, where he faces similar charges. The state case had been paused pending resolution of the federal proceedings, which concluded less than two weeks ago with Boelter's federal sentencing. Boelter's next state court date is set for September 2.

At Monday's hearing, Boelter questioned whether the court could compel U.S. Senator Amy Klobuchar to testify, claiming he had met with her and other Minnesota elected officials over eight years. He also told the judge his rights had been violated during his 14 months in federal custody; the judge directed him to raise any such arguments through his attorney at future hearings.

In state court, Boelter faces two counts of murder, four counts of attempted murder, impersonating a police officer, and animal cruelty after the Hortmans' golden retriever was gravely injured and later euthanized. State Sen. John Hoffman and his wife Yvette were critically wounded in the same attacks and have filed a separate civil lawsuit against Boelter. If convicted in state court, Boelter faces mandatory life without parole; Minnesota has no death penalty.

stories.headline: U.S. Resumes Deportation Flights to Venezuela for First Time Since June Earthquakes
stories.summary:
The United States sent a deportation flight carrying 147 Venezuelan nationals to Venezuela on Monday, resuming removals for the first time since devastating earthquakes struck the country in June. The resumption has drawn criticism from human rights advocates who have pointed to the deaths of deportees who were housed in a building that collapsed during the June earthquakes. Venezuela's National Assembly President Jorge Rodriguez has confirmed at least 6,125 people dead from those quakes, with the government's disaster response facing ongoing scrutiny.

Deportation flights to Venezuela had been a contested and intermittently halted policy before the earthquakes further complicated bilateral arrangements. Critics argue that returning migrants to a country still recovering from mass casualties and infrastructure collapse puts deportees at serious risk. The Trump administration has maintained that immigration enforcement continues regardless of conditions in receiving countries.

The resumed flights mark a significant development in U.S.-Venezuela relations and immigration enforcement policy, affecting a population that had previously been among the most difficult to deport due to strained diplomatic ties between the two governments.

stories.headline: Update: FIFA Crisis Deepens as Infantino Opponents Threaten 'Non-Cooperation'
stories.summary:
Opponents of FIFA president Gianni Infantino are threatening open "non-cooperation" with the governing body unless he resigns, according to senior UEFA sources, marking a significant escalation in the crisis over his scrapped plans to sell stakes in FIFA competitions to private investors. Senior figures involved in the rebellion say "there is no going back" while Infantino remains in office, with one source indicating they would "certainly expect" a refusal to participate in FIFA meetings.

The pressure on Infantino is intensifying across multiple fronts. Wales has publicly withdrawn backing for his re-election bid, with England's Football Association expected to follow. Serbia, Sweden and Finland have also withdrawn support, while the Asian Football Confederation has declared solidarity with UEFA and CONCACAF. Qatar, Morocco, Lebanon, Kuwait and Sri Lanka are among those still backing Infantino, who faces a re-election vote in March 2027 and needs 106 of FIFA's 211 member votes to win a fourth term.

UEFA has formally threatened legal action and arbitration over Infantino's proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise subsidiary, which would have allowed minority private investment in FIFA's main competitions including the World Cup. UEFA has also demanded FIFA preserve all relevant documents. A separate pathway exists to force Infantino out through an emergency council meeting, which would require 19 of the 37 FIFA Council members to call for one — a threshold that could be within reach given the breadth of the current rebellion.

stories.headline: Former Rep. Kay Granger, First Republican Woman from Texas in the House, Dies at 83
stories.summary:
Kay Granger, the first Republican woman elected to the U.S. House of Representatives from Texas and a 28-year congressional veteran, died Sunday at age 83, her son J.D. Granger announced. House Speaker Mike Johnson called her a trailblazer who "broke barriers for women in public service" and described her as "a dear friend who will be greatly missed."

Granger accumulated a series of historic firsts throughout her career. She was the first woman elected mayor of Fort Worth, Texas, serving from 1991 to 1995, and later became the first Republican woman to chair the powerful House Appropriations Committee. First elected to Congress in 1996, she did not seek reelection in 2024 after disclosing worsening health challenges. She had not cast a vote in Washington after July 2024.

Before entering politics, Granger worked as a high school English teacher and later built a successful insurance business as a single mother of three. She was recruited to run for Congress in 1996 by both parties before choosing to run as a Republican. During her tenure on the Appropriations Committee, she wielded significant influence over federal spending priorities.

stories.headline: Education Secretary McMahon Demands Universities Commit to Trump Reform Priorities by Year's End
stories.summary:
Education Secretary Linda McMahon sent an open letter Monday to university presidents and board members urging American colleges to formally outline their commitments to a set of Trump administration priorities — including national service, campus reforms, and other as-yet-specified principles — by the end of 2026. The move represents the administration's latest effort to reshape higher education after months of pressure on universities over issues including diversity programs, campus speech, and federal funding compliance.

McMahon's letter lamented that higher education institutions have, in her view, "drifted from the principles" that built them into respected institutions. The administration has deployed a range of tools to press universities into compliance with its agenda, including funding freezes and Title VI investigations, and the letter appears intended to create a transparency mechanism through which universities publicly state their positions.

Supporters of the administration's approach argue that universities have grown politically unaccountable and ideologically monolithic, and that public commitments to reform would restore balance and civic responsibility to campuses. Critics contend that the administration is using federal leverage to coerce academic institutions into ideological conformity, infringing on principles of academic freedom and institutional independence. The letter comes amid ongoing legal battles between the administration and several major universities over funding and accreditation.

stories.headline: Japan Mall Blast: Two Workers Died After Boss Ordered Re-entry to Secure Cash Following Earthquake
stories.summary:
Two workers killed in an explosion at the Aeon Mall in Kumamoto, Japan, last week died after their employer ordered them back into the earthquake-damaged building to move cash from a register into a safe, Japanese broadcaster NHK reported. The two employees were among 38 people killed by a magnitude 6.8 earthquake that struck Kumamoto prefecture on July 28; seven of the total fatalities occurred at the Aeon Mall.

One of the workers has been identified as 22-year-old Kurumi Otake, whose family told local media she encountered a relative outside the mall after the quake and said she had to return inside on her company's instructions. The employer, general goods retailer Habita, issued an apology, with sales director Goji Yuse telling reporters at Otake's wake: "Looking back now, it was not worth a life."

Most mall occupants had evacuated shortly after the initial earthquake, but some employees remained in the building approximately an hour later when a gas explosion tore through the structure. Habita said it was considering how to proceed in the aftermath, and the circumstances have prompted scrutiny of workplace safety protocols and employer obligations during natural disaster evacuations in Japan.

stories.headline: House Ethics Committee Recommends Censure of Rep. Chuck Edwards Over Sexual Harassment Violations
stories.summary:
The House Ethics Committee released a bipartisan report Monday recommending that Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) be formally censured by the full House after finding he violated House rules by failing to adhere to standards prohibiting sexual harassment and unwanted advances toward staff. The 25-page report concluded Edwards engaged in 'highly unprofessional' conduct with two young female staffers and that his behavior violated the Code of Official Conduct by failing to 'act in a manner that reflects creditably upon the House.' Edwards, who is married, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The committee, which operates on a bipartisan basis, found 'substantial reason to believe' Edwards violated House rules, stopping short of finding he engaged in direct sexual harassment but determining he violated the 'spirit' of those prohibitions. Censure is one of the most serious formal sanctions the House can impose on a sitting member, requiring a majority vote of the full chamber.

The recommendation now moves to the full House, where a vote on censure would put all members on record. Edwards represents North Carolina's 11th Congressional District. The case adds to a pattern of ethics investigations involving House members that has drawn attention from both parties in recent years.

stories.headline: Maryland Democrats Open Special Session on Constitutional Amendment to Enable Partisan Redistricting
stories.summary:
Maryland's General Assembly convened a special session Monday to begin debate on a constitutional amendment that would give Democratic lawmakers greater latitude to draw congressional maps favoring their party ahead of the 2028 election cycle. The proposed amendment would remove certain compactness and natural-boundary requirements from congressional redistricting, requirements a court previously used to strike down a 2021 Democratic gerrymander. If passed by three-fifths of both chambers, the measure would go before voters in November's general election.

Democratic state Senate President Bill Ferguson said his views on redistricting shifted after the U.S. Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act in late April, which he said enabled Republicans to rapidly redraw districts in Southern states in ways that disadvantaged minority voters. 'It felt like the unwinding of any type of democratic norms in the blink of an eye,' Ferguson said. Maryland currently sends seven Democrats and one Republican — Rep. Andy Harris, chair of the House Freedom Caucus — to the U.S. House.

Republicans have sharply criticized the effort, calling it a blatant partisan power grab. The move is part of a broader national redistricting battle that has already reshaped the U.S. House map ahead of this fall's midterm elections, with both parties drawing maps aggressively in states they control. Ferguson acknowledged that future map changes could depend on November's midterm outcomes.

stories.headline: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Sets All-Time North American Opening Weekend Record With $360 Million
stories.summary:
Sony Pictures' 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' broke the North American opening weekend box office record previously held by 'Avengers: Endgame,' earning $360 million in its debut weekend from 4,487 theaters across the U.S. and Canada, the studio announced Monday. The 2019 'Avengers: Endgame' record stood at $357 million; the new Spider-Man film surpassed it after a stronger-than-projected Sunday. Sony Pictures chairman Tom Rothman said, 'Records are made to be broken, but we will take great pride in this one, for as long as we hold it.'

The film stars Tom Holland in his fourth solo outing as Spider-Man, with Zendaya and Jon Bernthal also featured. Its opening surpasses all prior domestic records, including 'Avengers: Infinity War' ($257 million, 2018) and 'Star Wars: The Force Awakens' ($247 million, 2015). Combined with the simultaneous release of 'The Odyssey,' which shares several cast members, the weekend set an overall record for the domestic movie theater industry.

The milestone comes as the North American box office overall is tracking more than 15 percent ahead of last year, with over $6.2 billion in total ticket sales to date. The result is a significant boost for theatrical exhibition, which has faced structural headwinds from streaming competition in recent years.

stories.headline: Senate Reaches Bipartisan Deal to Avoid Government Shutdown
stories.summary:
Senate appropriators struck a bipartisan agreement Monday to fund the federal government through December 11, averting a potential government shutdown that could have coincided with midterm campaign season. The short-term continuing resolution is expected to come to a vote before the Senate departs for its August recess later this week.

The deal keeps agencies operating past the October deadline and removes a significant political liability for both parties as candidates focus on November midterm races. Leadership from both parties backed the measure, signaling rare cross-aisle cooperation on a fiscal deadline.

Government funding agreements typically draw support from both parties as neither side wants to be blamed for a shutdown heading into an election cycle. The measure will next face a House vote before it can be sent to the president for signature.

stories.headline: Fighting Erupts in Northern Ethiopia, Raising Fears of Return to Civil War
stories.summary:
Intense clashes broke out Saturday between the Tigray People's Liberation Front and the Ethiopian federal army near Shererina in western Tigray, near the border with Sudan. The fighting, which involved heavy artillery and drones and continued into Sunday, represents one of the most serious confrontations since a 2022 African Union-brokered peace deal ended a two-year civil war that killed hundreds of thousands of people.

Hundreds of civilians and wounded fighters have fled across the border into Sudan. Both sides have blamed each other for initiating hostilities: the TPLF-led regional administration accused the federal government of launching an "open war" aimed at "subjugating and dividing" the people of Tigray, while a federal minister accused the "TPLF clique" of starting the fight and warned of "worse consequences" if it continued.

The flare-up is alarming analysts because the 2022 peace deal has never been fully implemented, the TPLF recently retook control of Tigray after pushing out an interim administration, and there are fears the conflict could become a proxy battleground for warring factions in Sudan's own civil war. The death toll from the weekend's fighting remains unclear.

stories.headline: White House Finalizes AI Evaluation Framework but Keeps Contents Secret
stories.summary:
The White House announced Monday it had met its self-imposed deadline to establish a voluntary framework for evaluating advanced AI models, but declined to disclose what the framework contains, who has reviewed it, or when companies will be required to begin using it. The opaque rollout has drawn criticism from policymakers, AI safety advocates, and U.S. allies who have been waiting to see what guardrails would govern the world's most powerful AI systems.

The framework was developed largely behind closed doors and applies to frontier AI developers operating in the United States. Officials described it as a voluntary measure, though specifics about compliance mechanisms, participating companies, and timelines were not released alongside the announcement.

The secrecy surrounding the framework stands in contrast to the broad international attention the document has attracted. Advocates for AI safety have argued that transparency is essential for the framework to serve its intended purpose, while some industry representatives have previously pushed back against disclosure requirements that could reveal proprietary model information.

stories.headline: Rhine and Danube Hit Record Low Levels as European Drought Intensifies
stories.summary:
The Rhine River fell to record low levels at multiple measurement points in Germany and the Netherlands last week, with the critical chokepoint at Kaub near Koblenz matching the historic 2018 low of 25 centimeters before a slight recovery Monday. The Danube also hit its lowest levels in 30 years across Serbia, Romania, and Hungary, while Italy's Po River similarly registered record lows amid a prolonged drought affecting most of Europe.

The crisis is straining energy and industrial infrastructure across the continent. Hungary's sole nuclear power plant on the Danube is operating at reduced capacity and may need to be taken offline; Serbia cut output at coal-fired plants; and Romania conducted a controlled river-bank explosion to improve water flow to its Cernavoda nuclear facility. Two major car plants in Romania — operated by Dacia and Ford — agreed to halt production for more than two weeks to reduce electricity consumption.

Shipping on the Rhine, one of Europe's busiest commercial waterways, faces severe restrictions as low water levels force cargo operators to spread loads across more vessels, driving up transport costs and risking supply bottlenecks. German waterway authorities said shipping is unlikely to be suspended entirely but that precautions are necessary. The EU's Drought Observatory reported drought conditions worsened across central-western Europe through mid-July, with renewed heatwaves above 40°C forecast for at least another week.

stories.headline: Update: Blanche AG Nomination Advances After DOJ Formally Kills 'Anti-Weaponization' Fund
stories.summary:
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche formally rescinded the Trump administration's $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund on Monday, clearing the path for his Senate Judiciary Committee confirmation vote scheduled for Tuesday. The deal was brokered between Blanche and Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who had blocked the nomination alongside Sen. Thom Tillis over concerns about the fund, which was designed to compensate Trump allies for legal expenses.

The anti-weaponization fund had drawn bipartisan criticism, with Republican senators warning it represented an improper use of federal settlement dollars. President Trump acknowledged the fund is "dead" but expressed publicly that he wished it still existed — a rare instance of the president openly distancing himself from a concession made to secure a Cabinet confirmation.

The nomination's advancement represents a significant development for the Justice Department, which has operated under acting leadership for months. Democrats have opposed Blanche's confirmation, citing his prior role as Trump's personal defense attorney and concerns about the independence of the department under his leadership. Republicans broadly support confirmation, arguing the DOJ needs permanent leadership.

The Judiciary Committee vote Tuesday will determine whether Blanche advances to a full Senate floor vote. The resolution of the Cornyn standoff removes the most significant Republican obstacle to confirmation, making Blanche's path to becoming the nation's permanent attorney general substantially clearer.

stories.headline: Deadly Protests Grip Pakistan-Administered Kashmir as Elections Proceed Under Internet Blackout
stories.summary:
Dozens of people have been killed in Pakistan-administered Kashmir (PAK) over the past several weeks in clashes between security forces and protesters affiliated with the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a group demanding affordable electricity, flour, and basic rights guaranteed under a previous government agreement. The BBC gained rare first access to the city of Rawalakot, where a makeshift field clinic has treated 50 to 60 critically injured patients since July 27, including many with gunshot wounds, most of them young people between 15 and 35 years old.

The protests have coincided with regional elections, which authorities say are being disrupted by the JAAC. The government has labeled the group foreign-funded terrorists and banned it in June; the JAAC denies those characterizations, saying it is peaceful and that security forces have fired live ammunition at demonstrators. Internet access has been cut and roads blocked, severely restricting the flow of information out of the region.

The local government disputes accounts of indiscriminate violence, saying the group is armed and poses a security threat. Protesters say they fear going to major hospitals because they could be arrested or shot there — a claim authorities call inaccurate. The October agreement between the JAAC and both the Pakistani and PAK governments, which was meant to address grievances, has not been implemented according to the group.

The unrest in Pakistan-administered Kashmir, home to approximately 4.5 million people, highlights longstanding tensions over governance, economic conditions, and the disputed status of the region. The situation has drawn little international attention despite an escalating death toll and conditions that independent journalists have found extremely difficult to document.

stories.headline: SpaceX to Release First Quarterly Earnings Report as Public Company Tuesday
stories.summary:
SpaceX is set to issue its first quarterly earnings report as a public company on Tuesday afternoon, marking a significant milestone for the Elon Musk-led rocket, connectivity, and AI firm following the largest initial public offering on record in June. The company sold shares at $135 in its IPO, watched the stock surge past $225 in its early days, and has since fallen below its IPO price, touching a low of $107 last week amid operational setbacks and a broader pullback in AI-related equities.

The report arrives during a volatile period for tech and AI stocks more broadly. Major technology companies have been issuing new stock and taking on debt to finance expensive AI data center buildouts, raising investor questions about when those investments will generate returns. Several Magnificent 7 members, including Tesla, saw share price declines after signaling that their AI spending was far from complete.

SpaceX's earnings will be watched closely for signals about the health of the AI supply chain, as the company's satellite connectivity and computing infrastructure are deeply intertwined with the broader AI buildout. Chip and memory suppliers including Advanced Micro Devices and Western Digital also report this week, along with consumer names such as Spotify, Walt Disney, and McDonald's.

The week's earnings slate comes after a turbulent July for markets: the Nasdaq Composite fell 3.2% for the month, while the Dow edged higher and the S&P 500 ticked slightly lower. The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged last week, contributing to the Dow's worst single-day loss in 15 months before stocks partially recovered into the weekend.

stories.headline: India Exam Suicide Crisis: At Least 21 Students Dead After NEET Paper Leak Forces Re-Test
stories.summary:
At least 21 students in India died by suicide in the weeks surrounding the cancellation and rescheduling of the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), the country's medical school entrance examination, after a large-scale question paper leak forced nearly two million candidates to sit the exam again. The deaths, including that of 17-year-old Kahaan Patel of Ahmedabad who jumped from his family's apartment building three days before the rescheduled exam, became the emotional catalyst for a significant youth-led protest movement.

Thousands of students took to the streets of Delhi in July, demanding accountability for repeated failures in India's high-stakes exam system. The protests, partly organized through the satirical Cockroach Janta Party, resulted in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan — a rare instance of a senior Indian cabinet official stepping down under direct public pressure.

The NEET controversy exposes deep structural tensions in India's education system, where a single examination determines access to medical education for millions of aspirants who spend years and significant family resources preparing. Families like Kahaan Patel's relocated cities and reorganized their lives around the exam, making the leak and forced re-sit devastating beyond academic disappointment.

The crisis has prompted calls for systemic reform of India's centralized exam infrastructure and greater accountability for leaks. The scale of the upheaval — two million affected test-takers, a cabinet resignation, mass street protests, and dozens of deaths — makes it one of the most significant education-related crises in the country in recent memory.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Denies Trump's Claim That New Nuclear Talks Begin Monday
stories.summary:
Iran's Foreign Ministry on Monday flatly contradicted President Trump's assertion that new negotiations over the country's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz would begin that afternoon. Spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran was not negotiating with the United States and had no plans to do so, adding that Iran was engaged only with Oman over securing shipping passage through the strait. Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency called Trump's claims 'nothing but a new lie.'

Trump made the announcement aboard Air Force One on Sunday, saying Iran and U.S. allies in the Middle East had asked him to 'hold off' on strikes he described as potentially 'the biggest attack since World War Two.' He said the 'perimeters' of a deal had been agreed and that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, along with the UAE and Qatar, had urged restraint because 'they think there's a deal.' Iran's acting Defense Minister said Tehran viewed every threat as 'real and credible' and would 'neither be caught off guard nor remain passive.'

The contradictory statements mark another volatile turn in a conflict that has run since late February. Global oil prices fell sharply on Monday after Trump's announcement, with Brent Crude dropping 4.5 percent to $83.98 and U.S.-traded oil falling 4.6 percent to $80.74, reflecting market relief at the prospect of reduced military escalation even as the diplomatic picture remained deeply unclear.

The standoff directly affects roughly 20 percent of the world's crude oil and liquefied natural gas supply that normally transits the Strait of Hormuz. Trump's earlier calls-off of Iran strikes, contingent on a rapid nuclear deal, have previously been followed by resumed hostilities, and Tehran's denial on Monday raised fresh doubt about whether any negotiating framework exists.

stories.headline: Sudan Army Drone Strike on Village Court Session Kills 35
stories.summary:
A Sudanese army drone strike on a traditional court session held under a tree in the village of Ghara al-Zawiya, in northern Darfur, killed at least 35 people and wounded dozens more on Sunday afternoon, according to the Emergency Lawyers Group, a local organization that monitors civilian casualties. Four tribal leaders and two commanders from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces were among the dead. The Sudanese army has not commented on the strike.

Ghara al-Zawiya is held by the RSF, which controls most of Darfur as the two sides continue a three-year civil war that has killed tens of thousands and displaced millions. The Emergency Lawyers Group condemned the attack as a 'grave violation of international humanitarian law' and called for an investigation, noting that drones are being 'increasingly used to target civilian areas and gatherings.'

The RSF has itself been accused of war crimes, including drone strikes on civilians, and a UN fact-finding mission last year said its siege of the city of el-Fasher bore 'hallmarks of genocide.' Both sides deny targeting civilians. The latest strike underscores the war's continuing toll on Darfur's civilian population and the absence of any ceasefire or peace process.

stories.headline: Wildfires Force 60,000 to Evacuate Spokane; At Least 600 Structures Destroyed
stories.summary:
Wildfires burning in and around Spokane, Washington, forced the evacuation of roughly 60,000 people and destroyed at least 600 homes, businesses, and other structures over the weekend, state and local officials said Sunday. The fires burned approximately 8.2 square miles in the Spokane area alone and remained uncontained. Evacuees included patients at the city's Veterans Affairs hospital, and officials said dry weather conditions in the days ahead were expected to keep the danger elevated.

Across Washington state, about 390 square miles had burned, and dozens of additional wildfires were stretching the capacity of federal, state, and local firefighting agencies. Separately, crews were in their tenth day battling a fire that had consumed nearly 525 square miles of grassland straddling western Idaho and eastern Oregon, threatening more than 600 homes and 800 other structures in ranch country. Investigators had not yet determined the cause of the Spokane-area fires.

Washington Governor spoke with President Trump about the disaster, and U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell warned at a Spokane news conference that 'we are not out of danger.' No injuries or missing persons had been reported as of Sunday, though officials cautioned it was early in the response. The fires are among the most destructive to hit the Spokane area in recent memory.

stories.headline: Aung San Suu Kyi Seen in Public for First Time in Nearly Four Years After ICRC Visit
stories.summary:
Detained Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi, 81, has been seen in photographs for the first time in nearly four years after a delegation from the International Committee of the Red Cross was permitted to visit her, the ICRC confirmed Monday. Images released by Myanmar's military government show Suu Kyi appearing healthy and relaxed with ICRC representative Arnaud de Baecque. The visit marks the first confirmed outside contact since a letter she sent to her son more than two and a half years ago.

Suu Kyi was detained following the military coup that deposed her government in February 2021 and sentenced to 33 years in prison on charges widely regarded as politically motivated, though her sentence has since been reduced and she was moved to house arrest. Her son Kim Aris had mounted an international campaign in recent months demanding proof of life. He welcomed Monday's news as 'the first positive development for his mother in more than five years' but said it 'must not be the last.'

The ICRC said the visit was conducted according to its standard procedures for visiting detainees and included private time with Suu Kyi, though no details of her health or the content of discussions were disclosed. Myanmar's military government, which held elections earlier this year while continuing to conduct aerial bombardments of opposition areas, has faced international demands to release Suu Kyi and negotiate an end to the ongoing civil war. The publication of the visit photographs is being read by analysts as a possible signal that the junta may be willing to ease conditions of her detention.
